item.title: 2026 is deadliest start to a year for Mediterranean migrants, UN says
item.description:
The United Nations' International Organization for Migration announced Monday that at least 606 migrants have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean Sea since the beginning of 2026, making it the deadliest start to a year since the agency began tracking such data in 2014.

The grim milestone came as search operations continued off the Greek island of Crete, where a vessel carrying roughly 50 people capsized on Saturday approximately 20 nautical miles south of the port of Kali Limenes. Twenty people were rescued, including four minors, and the bodies of three men and one woman were recovered, according to the Associated Press. About 30 others remain unaccounted for.

item.title: Waterloo researchers turn plastic waste into vinegar using sunlight
item.description: Researchers at the University of Waterloo have developed a sunlight-driven process that converts plastic waste, including microplastics, into acetic acid — the main component of vinegar — using a catalyst inspired by the way fungi break down organic matter in nature.

item.title: EU leaders visit Kyiv as Ukraine marks four years of war
item.description:
On Tuesday, February 24, 2026 — exactly four years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion — Ukraine entered a fifth year of fighting with no end in sight, as its people continue to endure daily bombardment, displacement, and an energy crisis that has left millions shivering through one of the harshest winters in recent memory.

Senior European Union leaders traveled to Kyiv to mark the occasion. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa attended an official memorial ceremony, visited energy infrastructure damaged by Russian missile strikes, and held a trilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Coalition of the Willing, a group of 35 countries convened by British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron, held a videoconference reaffirming support for Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte participated in a separate ceremony at NATO headquarters in Brussels.

item.title: Russian oil exports top prewar levels despite four years of sanctions
item.description:
Four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the volume of Russian crude oil being shipped abroad remains above prewar levels, even as the revenue Moscow earns from those barrels has fallen sharply, according to new data published on the fourth anniversary of the conflict.

The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a Finland-based think tank known as CREA, reported on Tuesday that Russian crude oil export volumes in the 12 months ending February 24, 2026, remained six percent above pre-invasion levels, totaling 215 million tonnes. Yet revenues from those crude exports dropped 18 percent year-on-year to 85.5 billion euros, as Russia has been forced to sell at steep discounts to attract buyers. Total fossil fuel export revenues fell to an estimated 193 billion euros for the period, down 27 percent from comparable pre-invasion levels.

item.title: Ukraine reconstruction costs hit $588B as war marks four years
item.description:
As Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine enters its fifth year on February 24, 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the war "a stain on our collective consciousness" and renewed his demand for "an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire" as a first step toward lasting peace. In remarks to the Human Rights Council on Monday, Guterres noted that more than 15,000 civilians have been killed and declared: "It is more than past time to end the bloodshed".

The anniversary comes days after the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine ended without a breakthrough in Geneva, where negotiations on territorial control and security guarantees remain at an impasse.

item.title: Explosion near Moscow train station kills police officer on Ukraine war anniversary
item.description:
An unidentified assailant detonated an explosive device beside a police patrol vehicle at Savyolovsky Station Square in central Moscow early Tuesday, killing himself and a traffic police officer and wounding two others, Russian authorities said. The blast came just minutes into February 24 — the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The attack occurred at approximately 00:05 Moscow time, according to Moscow's branch of the Interior Ministry, which said the man approached officers sitting inside a patrol car before the device went off. One officer was killed instantly, while two others were hospitalized.

item.title: Rival studies clash over fate of massive dying star WOH G64
item.description:
WOH G64, one of the most extreme stars ever observed, is at the center of a scientific debate over whether it is on a path toward imminent destruction or simply behaving strangely under the influence of a companion star.

A study published February 23 in Nature Astronomy by a team led by Gonzalo Muñoz-Sanchez concludes that WOH G64 has undergone a "dramatic transition" from a red supergiant to a yellow hypergiant, a rare and unstable phase that can precede a supernova explosion. The researchers analyzed more than three decades of photometric and spectroscopic data, finding that the star's effective temperature increased by more than 1,000 degrees Kelvin since roughly 2014. They describe WOH G64 as a "rare, massive symbiotic binary system" and propose that the transition could result from the partial ejection of its outer envelope or the winding down of a decades-long eruption.

item.title: Oil prices near 7-month highs as U.S.-Iran talks loom
item.description:
Oil prices hovered near seven-month highs on Tuesday as traders weighed the prospect of a new round of U.S.-Iran nuclear talks against an increasingly bellicose tone from President Donald Trump, who warned Tehran of a "very bad day" if negotiations fail.

Brent crude futures rose 0.8% to $72.08 a barrel in early Asian trade on Tuesday, nearing their highest level since late July, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude climbed 0.9% to $66.88 a barrel. Both benchmarks had touched their firmest levels in roughly seven months during Monday's session, with Brent reaching $72.50 and WTI hitting $67.28, before pulling back.

item.title: Bitcoin drops below $63,000 as Trump's 15% tariff takes effect
item.description:
Bitcoin tumbled more than 5% on Tuesday, sliding below $63,000 as a new round of global tariffs took effect and escalating tensions in the Middle East pushed investors further away from risk assets. The leading cryptocurrency fell to a low of $62,964.64, according to CNBC, as market participants engaged in what analysts described as broad "tactical de-risking."

The drop coincided with the midnight implementation of President Donald Trump's 15% global import tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 — a statute never before invoked by a president. Trump signed the measure on February 20, initially setting the rate at 10%, before raising it to the statutory maximum of 15% the following day via a post on Truth Social. The move came just hours after the U.S. Supreme Court, in a 6-3 ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, struck down the administration's previous tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

item.title: MIT study rules out wildfires, volcanoes as cause of recent surface warming
item.description:
A team of MIT scientists has isolated the distinct global temperature effects of three landmark natural events — the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo, the 2019-2020 Australian wildfires, and the 2022 Hunga Tonga underwater volcanic eruption — using decades of satellite data and a novel signal-to-noise approach, according to a study published this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The findings show that while all three events left measurable marks on atmospheric temperatures, none appear to explain the accelerating warming trend at Earth's surface in recent years, pointing instead to human activity as the dominant driver.

item.title: Asian markets split as AI fears, new tariffs rattle investors
item.description:
Asian stocks diverged on Tuesday as markets across the region absorbed a sharp Wall Street selloff driven by fresh concerns about artificial intelligence displacing legacy businesses, while a new 10% global tariff imposed by President Donald Trump took effect just days after the Supreme Court struck down his original trade duties.

Japan's Nikkei 225 surged 0.9% to 57,354 as markets reopened from a holiday, lifted by gains in semiconductor-related stocks. South Korea's Kospi climbed 1.8% to a record 5,951.90, powered by Samsung Electronics, which jumped 3.2%, and SK Hynix, up 4.8%. Mainland China also rallied on its return from Lunar New Year, with the Shanghai Composite rising 1.2%. But Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.9% to 26,564 as traders locked in profits from a recent rally.

item.title: Oil tanker costs hit 6-year high as US-Iran war fears mount
item.description: Oil prices are hovering near seven-month highs and the cost of chartering supertankers has tripled since the start of the year as the threat of military conflict between the United States and Iran rattles global energy markets. The surge reflects a deepening risk premium across the oil supply chain, driven not by actual supply losses but by the prospect of disruption to the world's most critical crude chokepoint.

item.title: Iran nears deal to buy supersonic missiles from China
item.description: Iran is close to finalizing an agreement with China to purchase CM-302 supersonic anti-ship cruise missiles, according to a Reuters report citing six people with knowledge of the negotiations. The deal would represent one of the most advanced military transfers between the two countries and comes as the United States positions a vast naval force near Iran's coastline amid escalating tensions over Tehran's nuclear program.

item.title: Russia warns US nuclear testing would trigger 'domino effect'
item.description: The United States on Monday doubled down on accusations that China conducted a secret underground nuclear test in 2020, presenting what it called newly declassified intelligence at the United Nations Conference on Disarmament in Geneva as it pushed for broader multilateral arms control negotiations.

item.title: Meta signs 6-gigawatt AI chip deal with AMD
item.description:
Meta Platforms and AMD on Tuesday announced a multi-year, multi-generation agreement to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPUs for Meta's AI infrastructure, in a deal that could generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue for the chipmaker and reshape the competitive landscape of the AI hardware market.

The partnership marks Meta's most direct move yet to diversify its AI compute supply chain beyond Nvidia, which secured its own sweeping deal with Meta just one week earlier. Under the agreement, AMD issued Meta a performance-based warrant for up to 160 million shares of AMD common stock — roughly 10% of the company — structured to vest as shipment milestones and stock price thresholds are achieved.

item.title: U.S. details alleged secret Chinese nuclear test, urges disarmament talks
item.description: A senior American arms control official on Monday presented newly declassified details of what Washington says was a secret Chinese underground nuclear test conducted in 2020, urging the international community to pressure Beijing and Moscow toward nuclear disarmament just weeks after the last remaining U.S.-Russia arms treaty expired.

item.title: King's College London creates first-ever aluminum compound to rival platinum catalysts
item.description:
Chemists at King's College London have isolated a new form of aluminum that could offer a cheaper and more sustainable alternative to precious metals widely used in industrial catalysis. The work, led by Dr. Clare Bakewell, a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Chemistry, describes the first-ever cyclotrialumane — a compound made of three aluminum atoms arranged in a triangular structure — capable of breaking apart tough chemical bonds.

Published in Nature Communications, the research comes at a time when supply chain disruptions and soaring costs for precious metals like platinum and palladium are forcing the chemical industry to search for abundant alternatives.

item.title: US and NATO launch major Arctic exercises amid rising tensions
item.description: The Arctic has emerged as a theater of intensifying military competition and environmental upheaval, with NATO launching new operations, the United States conducting exercises spanning Alaska and Greenland, and Russia and China deepening their joint presence across the region — all as record-breaking warmth reshapes the polar landscape.

item.title: Russia opens criminal case against Telegram's Durov
item.description:
Russia has launched a criminal investigation into Pavel Durov, the founder and chief executive of Telegram, on charges of facilitating terrorist activities, the state-run newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta reported on Tuesday, citing evidence from the Federal Security Service (FSB). The move marks a sharp escalation in Moscow's increasingly confrontational campaign against the messaging platform and its Dubai-based founder.

"The actions of the head of Telegram, P. Durov, are being investigated as part of a criminal case on the grounds of a crime under Part 1.1 of Article 205.1 (assistance to terrorist activities) of the Criminal Code of Russia," Rossiyskaya Gazeta reported in an article it said was "based on materials from the FSB of Russia." The charge carries a potential sentence of eight years to life imprisonment.

Durov responded to the announcement on his Telegram channel. "Russia has opened a criminal case against me for aiding terrorism," he wrote, describing the investigation as pressure on the messenger service.

item.title: Russia losing troops faster than it can replace them, Western officials say
item.description:
On the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western officials disclosed that Moscow's battlefield losses have outpaced its ability to recruit replacements for three consecutive months, a development that could reshape the trajectory of the conflict.

Since November, Russian forces have suffered nearly 40,000 casualties per month while managing to enlist only about 35,000 new troops, according to Western officials cited by The Telegraph. The growing deficit marks what analysts describe as a potential turning point in Europe's largest land war since 1945.
